newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Quakes in Iran, Pakistan kill 150.
newsitem.headline: Quakes in Iran, Pakistan kill 150.

text.p: Two violent earthquakes hit southwestern Pakistan and neighbouring Iran in quick succession on Friday, killing about 150 people and injuring hundreds more.

The first quake struck in Pakistan's Baluchistan province in the early hours, waking residents in the provincial capital of Quetta with a roar "like doomsday". About 16 hours later, a tremor measuring 5.5 on the Richter scale shook northwestern Iran near the border with Azerbaijan.
The Iranian quake was the deadliest, according to initial casualty reports, with state television saying at least 100 people died and 250 were injured.

In Pakistan, local officials said at least 48 people were killed and more than 100 injured. But they added that the death toll could rise further as information came in from stricken villages in difficult mountainous terrain.
Officials at the U.S. Geological Survey's National Earthquake Information Centre in Golden, Colorado, said they saw no link between the two quakes.
"I don't think they're related at all," Director Waverly Person said. "Both areas are active seismically," he said, adding that the timing was a coincidence.
The Iranian quake hit the city of Ardabil and the town of Meshkinshahr at 4.27 p.m. (1257 GMT), state television said.

"The country's Natural Disaster Headquarters announced, with regret, that at least 100 of our compatriots have lost their lives and over 250 people were injured," said the television, monitored by the British Broadcasting Corporation.
The quake lasted 30 seconds and caused considerable damage in many of the surrounding districts in Ardabil province which borders Azerbaijan, it said.
Rescue teams rushed to the stricken areas to help the survivors, the television said.
Ardabil is an agricultural province inhabited mainly by Iran's Azeri minority. It is one of Iran's coldest regions with regular freezing temperatures during the winter.
In Pakistan, the private Edhi ambulance centre in Quetta put the death toll as high as 65, a figure which could not be confirmed from government sources.
That quake struck at 2.10 a.m. (2110 GMT Thursday). Another big jolt followed 20 minutes later and milder tremors continued for two hours, witnesses said.
"I thought doomsday had arrived and the world was about to end," said Feroza Begum, a schoolteacher in Quetta.

The highest casualties occurred in three villages near Harnai town, about 100 km (63 miles) east of Quetta, where at least 38 people were killed and about 100 injured, a senior provincial government official said.
Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif ordered a massive relief effort for the quake victims.

A government seismic centre in the northwestern town of Peshawar measured the earthquake at 6.2 on the Richter scale. It placed the epicentre in the Koh-i-Suleman mountain range, north of Quetta, near the Afghan border.
In Quetta, the quake drove terrified residents, hotel guests and even hospital patients outside to spend the rest of the night with quilts and blankets to ward off the freezing cold.

Moslem clerics went to mosques and called the faithful to prayer, a traditional response to calamity. Men fired guns in the air to wake people up. Officials used loudspeakers to warn people not to stay indoors because of the risk of more tremors.
Quetta was destroyed by an earthquake on May 31, 1935 that measured 7.5 on the Richter scale and killed 30,000 people.

The Iranian news agency IRNA said a third quake measuring 5.5 on the Richter scale hit the western Iranian city of Sanandaj at about the same time as the tremor hit Ardabil, some 350 km (220 miles) away.
There were no immediate reports of casualties or damage in Sanandaj, a Kurdish-populated provincial capital, it said.
Tremors of four and five on the Richter scale can be powerful enough to cause heavy damage in populated areas.
In early February, two earthquakes measuring 6.1 and 5.4 killed at least 79 people and injured 260 in a mountainous region in northeastern Iran.
Earthquakes hit Iran regularly. The worst recorded one, measuring 7.3 on the Richter scale, killed 35,000 people in Gilan and neighbouring Zanjan province in 1990.
